chunks.text: Wastewater is typically collected through sewage pipes in municipal areas. Treatment of wastewater entails a step-wise process that occurs in primary, secondary, and tertiary stages. Primary treatment involves basic screening and filtration processes to remove suspended solid waste and reduce its biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), which is an indicator to monitor water quality that assesses the amount of oxygen microorganisms must consume to break down the organic material present in wastewater (US EPA, 2012) . Primary treatment can reduce BOD by up to 30% (Flo ¨rke, 2013) . Secondary treatment uses biological processes to break down the dissolved organic matter remaining after primary treatment. Secondary treatment can remove up to 90% of BOD and total suspended solids (US EPA, 2004) . Any additional step in wastewater treatment is considered tertiary treatment (or ''advanced treatment''), which includes any purification process that continues beyond the previous steps and may require more complex technology such as ion exchange and reverse osmosis to further remove contaminants or phosphorous and nitrogen (World Bank, 2013b; US EPA, 2004) .

The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . This model uses thirteen state variables to track the fate of biodegradable, non-biodegradable, soluble, insoluble, nitrogen, and carbon materials. These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.text: In order to recover the lipid-rich biomass from the treated wastewaters and to further reduce the level of COD in the respective wastewaters, microfiltration using a low-cost ceramic membrane (pore size: 1.01 μm and porosity: 44%) was carried out. Fig. 6 presents the membrane flux and COD removal (%) from the different wastewaters at various operating pressures in the range of 34-172 kPa. With an increase in the operating pressure, the flux of the microfiltration system increased due to a high driving force acting on the membrane surface. The membrane flux was lower for DWW and PPWW as compared with that for the BGWW due to membrane fouling. In general, the membrane fouling is attributed to concentration polarization on the membrane surface and blocking of pores in the porous ceramic structure. In case of DWW and PPWW, fouling of the membrane was observed due to the adsorption of organic solutes/lignin and membrane surface polarization that creates further resistance to the transport of liquid through the membrane [1] . On the other hand, the less viscous BGWW possesses persistent organics [22] , and hence do not affect the membrane flux largely.

chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

chunks.text: Anaerobic digestion (AD), an anoxic biological wastewater treatment process, is widely implemented to reduce the organic load of LW. It was the third most used process in the selected references. During AD, a gas mixture (biogas) and an effluent (digestate) are produced. The biogas, primarily composed of CH 4 and CO 2 , can be used to produce energy. The effluent, known as digestate or anaerobically digested livestock wastewater (ADLW), requires further treatment before being reused or discharged due to its high content of organic matter, N, P, and pathogens (Huo et al., 2021) . Wang et al. (2022a) conducted a full-scale microalgal electroactive wetland coupled with AD to treat SW. The AD achieved removal efficiencies of 77-89% CODr, 27-30% TPr, 26-73% NH 4 + -N removal, and 50-63% TNr. These efficiencies were temperature-dependent, with higher values in summer and spring, and lower in autumn and winter.

chunks.text: The treatment processes in the centralized WWTP consisted of pretreatment, primary treatment, biological secondary treatment (activated sludge), chlorine disinfection, and anaerobic digestion of solids. The utility operates a combined sewer system that captures both sewage and stormwater flows. In dry weather, the average concentrations of BOD 5 and TSS in the inflow wastewater of the centralized WWTP are 228 mg/L and 248 mg/L. The average dry-weather flow is 65.3 MGD (250 ML/day). In wet weather, BOD 5 and TSS concentrations are 171 mg/L and 147 mg/L. The average wet-weather flow is 119 MGD (450 ML/ day). The wastewater passes through bar screens followed by a grit removal process to remove large debris and inert solids, and then is directed to primary clarifiers for the removal of settleable solids and floatables. The primary effluent flows to the activated sludge process composed of six stages. The first two stages of the activated sludge system function as an anaerobic selector, and pure oxygen is introduced in the subsequent stages. The effluent from the aeration basins flows to 16 circular secondary clarifiers.

chunks.text: The main objective of primary treatment of wastewater is the removal of settleable organic and inorganic solids by sedimentation and skimming. Here, about 50 to 60% of the total suspended solids (SS), and 65% of the oil and grease are removed along with some organic nitrogen, phosphorous, and heavy metals attached to the solids. However, the colloidal particles and dissolved constituents are not removed in this stage. Generally, gravity separation is employed in this step to separate the biosolids using either coagulation, flocculation, flotation or filtration techniques as seen in Fig. 2 . However, recent innovations in efficient wastewater treatment have brought advancements in this area (Table 4 ). For example, Salsnes filter system reported to have only 1/10th of land requirement and offers 30-60% lower investment and operating costs as compared to a conventional primary treatment system (Trojan Technologies, 2012).

chunks.text: The secondary biological treatment consists of two carrousel-shaped biological reactors with suspended biomass, equipped with two horizontal aerators, which include nitrogen removal. Regarding the sludge line, a fraction of the solids settled in the secondary settler is purged to the sludge thickener. Previously to the band filter, the sludge passes through a homogenizer to be mixed with cationic polyelectrolyte and further dewatered in the band filter prior being stored in a silo. Calafell WWTP was built on 1994 to treat the wastewaters of the municipalities of Calafell and Bellveí and designed for 70,000 population equivalent with a maximum flow of 12,000 m 3 /day. After a primary treatment, wastewater is treated in two activated sludge reactors with extended aeration including nitrogen removal, followed by the secondary settler. From these units, the treated wastewater is directly discharged to the submarine sewage. Some differences are observed in the operation of the plant between winter and summer seasons due to fluctuations on the population and changes on the influent composition. A coagulation-flocculation treatment, only operated during summer, receives the wastewater after the screening step.

chunks.text: A mass of 300 kg of screenings was sampled from the municipal wastewater treatment plant of Bourg-en-Bresse (Region Rhône-   Alpes, France). The waste was made of a mix of screenings from 15-mm and 3-mm screens and was compacted in the plant. The sample was taken to the laboratory where it was homogenized and divided into 20 sub-samples of 8 kg. The procedure allowed to guarantee a good reproducibility of the sub-samples composition, which was verified analytically. The samples were stored at À18 °C. A digestate sampled from a municipal solid waste (MSW) digester was used as an inoculum, in order to have active microflora and to make easier the start-up of anaerobic process.
